headline: Moon contracts, falling gold and a snake’s second chance
teaser: Should private companies build our Moon Base? Why would a central bank buy gold as prices fall? And can captive breeding save a rare snake?

articles.title: Building a Base on the Moon, One Contract at a Time
articles.dek: NASA is paying private companies to help build a Moon Base. Is buying services from industry the smartest way to explore space, or a risky bet?
paras: On November 7, at an aerospace exhibition at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida, NASA announced a package of contracts that brings its plan for a permanent Moon Base a step closer to reality. The awards range from a nuclear-powered rover to a ten-year agreement under which private companies will compete to deliver cargo to the lunar surface. “We are building the Moon Base mission by mission,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. The announcement offers a clear picture of how the agency now hopes to explore space: not by building everything itself, but by buying services from industry.

For most of the space age, NASA designed and owned its own rockets and spacecraft. The Apollo missions that landed astronauts on the Moon between 1969 and 1972 were government projects from start to finish. Over the past two decades, however, the agency has gradually shifted toward a commercial model. Instead of building hardware, it signs contracts with companies that design their own vehicles and are paid for delivering results. The Commercial Lunar Payload Services program, known as CLPS, applied this idea to the Moon by paying firms to carry NASA instruments to the lunar surface.

The largest of the new awards extends that approach. NASA selected eight companies, including SpaceX, Blue Origin, Firefly Aerospace and Intuitive Machines, for a follow-on program called CLPS 2. Over ten years, these firms will compete for individual delivery missions worth a combined maximum of $10 billion. This figure is a ceiling rather than a guaranteed payment; companies receive money only when they win specific missions. At the same time, NASA raised the value of the original CLPS contract from $2.6 billion to $4.2 billion.

The most eye-catching project is a six-wheeled rover called PROMISE, which will explore the Moon’s south pole. Because it will be nuclear-powered, it is designed to keep working through the long, freezing lunar night and inside craters that never see sunlight, where solar panels would be useless. Engineers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory will build it partly from spare parts and test models left over from the Curiosity and Perseverance Mars rovers, an approach intended to reduce both cost and risk. Its drill will reach about one meter below the surface. Blue Origin received a $94 million base contract, with an option worth up to $140 million more, to land the rover on the Moon in late 2028.

Other awards fill in the supporting pieces. About $1.3 billion in task orders will pay three companies to launch and transport cargo, including small drones designed to survey the south pole. SpaceX will use its giant Starship rocket to place communications satellites in cislunar space, the region between Earth and the Moon, in 2028. Three more firms will develop a solar-powered tower that provides both electricity and communications for equipment on the surface.

Supporters argue that this model is the fastest and most affordable way to build a lasting presence on the Moon. Competition, they say, pushes companies to cut costs and innovate, and firms that own their vehicles can sell services to other customers, spreading the expense. Reusing Mars rover parts and buying launches rather than building rockets allows NASA to focus its limited budget on science. In Isaacman’s words, when astronauts eventually return, they “will arrive with the first elements of the Moon Base already waiting for them.”

Yet the approach carries real risks. When NASA buys a service, it gives up some control over design and schedules, and commercial lunar landers have a mixed record: several recent missions have tipped over or crashed while landing. Many of the vehicles in the plan, including Starship and Blue Origin’s lander, are still being tested, so a delay at one company could ripple through the whole program. Nuclear power also raises questions. Although nuclear power sources have run safely on Mars rovers for years, launching radioactive material will always require careful oversight and public trust.

In the end, NASA’s announcement is less a single breakthrough than a bet on a particular way of exploring. If the commercial model works, the Moon could host a steady stream of robots, instruments and eventually people within a decade. If it falters, the agency may discover that outsourcing saves money only when everything goes to plan. For now, the contracts suggest that the return to the Moon will be shaped not only by rocket science, but also by how wisely the work is shared.

speak.p: Some people think space exploration should be carried out mainly by government agencies. Others believe private companies can do it better and more cheaply. Which view do you agree with, and why? Use specific reasons and examples.
speak.hint: Give your view → reason 1 (cost/speed or safety/control) + example → reason 2 + example → short conclusion.

write.p: Professor: NASA is now paying private companies to deliver cargo, launch satellites and even land a nuclear-powered rover on the Moon. Supporters say competition makes space exploration faster and cheaper. Critics say important public projects should stay under government control. Should governments rely on private companies for big public projects like this? Why or why not? (Mia says: Companies have to compete, so they work harder to cut costs and find new ideas. NASA can then spend its money on science instead of building rockets.) (Daniel says: When a company fails or is delayed, the whole public project suffers. Safety-critical work, like launching nuclear material, should be controlled directly by the government.)
steps: State your position in one clear sentence.
Give one reason with a concrete example (cost, speed, safety, accountability).
Respond to Mia or Daniel: agree with part of their point, then add a new idea.
Finish with a short concluding sentence.

articles.title: Buying When Prices Fall: Why China’s Central Bank Keeps Adding Gold
articles.dek: Gold just had its worst October since 2008, yet China’s central bank kept buying. Is gold smart insurance or an outdated asset that earns nothing?
paras: Gold had a terrible October. Its price fell by nearly 7 percent during the month, the steepest October drop since 2008, and slipped below $4,000 an ounce, its lowest level in a year. Many private investors sold. Yet one of the world’s most powerful financial institutions did the opposite. According to official data released on November 7, the People’s Bank of China, the country’s central bank, added about 25.8 tonnes of gold to its reserves in October, extending its buying streak to 24 consecutive months.

To understand why this matters, it helps to know what central banks do with their reserves. Every central bank holds a stockpile of foreign currencies and other assets, known as foreign exchange reserves. These reserves can be used to stabilize the national currency, pay for imports during a crisis, or reassure markets that the country can meet its obligations. Most reserves are held in major currencies, especially the US dollar, often in the form of government bonds. Gold is a smaller but symbolically important part of the mix, because its value is not tied to any single government’s promises.

China’s purchases have been steady rather than dramatic. The central bank now reports holdings of about 78.3 million ounces, roughly 2,400 tonnes. It bought about 63 tonnes in the third quarter, the most of any central bank that publicly reported its purchases, and roughly 129 tonnes in the first ten months of the year. China is not alone: according to the World Gold Council, central banks around the world bought a net 321 tonnes between July and September, the largest quarterly total since late 2024.

Why would a central bank keep buying an asset whose price is falling? One explanation is diversification. A reserve portfolio concentrated in one currency is exposed to that currency’s risks, including changes in the issuing country’s interest rates or policies. Gold offers a form of protection that does not depend on another government, and the World Gold Council lists safety and liquidity among the qualities central banks value in it. From this point of view, a lower price is not a warning sign but an opportunity: the bank can buy more gold for the same amount of money.

A second explanation concerns long-term planning. Central banks do not trade like individual investors who hope to profit within weeks. They think in decades, and small, regular purchases smooth out the effect of short-term price swings, a strategy sometimes compared to saving a fixed amount each month. Officially, however, Beijing rarely explains its reasoning, and the data alone cannot reveal the exact balance between these motives.

There are also costs and risks. Gold pays no interest, unlike government bonds, so every tonne bought means giving up a steady income. Its price can also be extremely volatile, as October showed. Because of the fall in prices, the reported value of China’s gold reserves dropped from about $323.5 billion at the end of September to $306.4 billion a month later, even though the bank owned more gold. There are reasons, too, not to read too much into the purchases. China’s foreign exchange reserves total about $3.4 trillion, more than ten times the value of its gold, and the dollar remains by far the world’s dominant reserve currency.

Central bank demand nevertheless has real effects on the market. Bloomberg has described continued official buying as a key support for prices in a weak market, since it creates steady demand when other buyers retreat. Ordinary Chinese savers also reportedly bought gold around the $4,000 level in October, suggesting that some households share the view that falling prices are a chance to buy rather than a reason to panic.

The story of China’s gold purchases therefore raises a broader question about value and trust. Is gold a relic of the past, an asset that earns nothing and swings wildly in price, or a form of insurance whose worth becomes clear only in a crisis? Different institutions answer that question differently, and their choices reflect how they see the risks ahead. For students of economics, the lesson is that a market price tells only part of the story; the reasons behind each decision to buy or sell matter just as much.

speak.p: Some people prefer to keep their savings in safe assets like gold or bank deposits. Others prefer riskier investments that may earn more money. Which approach do you think is better for a young person, and why? Use specific reasons and examples.

write.p: Professor: Central banks such as China’s have been buying gold for two years, even when prices fall. Some economists say gold is reliable insurance in an uncertain world. Others call it an outdated asset because it earns no interest and its price swings wildly. Is gold still a sensible thing for countries to hold today? Explain your view. (Sofia says: Gold has kept its value for thousands of years and does not depend on any government. In a crisis, it is the safest thing a country can own.) (Kevin says: Gold earns nothing, and October showed how quickly its value can fall. Countries would do better to hold bonds that pay interest every year.)
steps: Give your view in one sentence.
Support it with one reason and an example (a crisis, a price fall, interest income).
Respond to Sofia or Kevin, agreeing with part of their idea before adding something new.

articles.title: Rocks, Rescue and Risk: Returning an Endangered Snake to the Wild
articles.dek: Six captive-bred snakes were released into the wild near Sydney, and most have survived. Is breeding animals in captivity the answer, or should we protect their homes first?
paras: In the sandstone cliffs south of Sydney, Australia, six young snakes have been doing something no member of their species had done before: living in the wild after being born in captivity. Researchers from the University of Technology Sydney and the conservation group Aussie Ark announced on November 6 that at least four of the six endangered broad-headed snakes released in May had survived their first months outside. The number is small, but the result is being described as a world first for the species.

The broad-headed snake is one of Australia’s most threatened reptiles. It is found only in the rocky escarpments of the Sydney sandstone basin and nearby ranges, where it shelters in cracks and under flat rocks. The species grows to about 90 centimeters long, is venomous, and hunts mainly small lizards that live among the rocks. Its biology makes it especially vulnerable: snakes take around five years to reach adulthood, and females breed only every two or three years. Even small losses can therefore take decades to recover from.

Several pressures have pushed the species toward the edge. The severe drought of 2017 to 2019 and the bushfires of 2020 hit populations hard; researchers recorded a decline of about 64 percent between the drought and 2023, and little breeding was observed for three years after the fires. A more surprising threat is human demand for garden decoration. Natural “bush rock” is collected from the wild for landscaping, and a single attractive boulder can sell for hundreds of dollars. Removing these rocks destroys the shelters the snakes depend on, along with the lizards they eat. The state of New South Wales listed bush-rock removal as a key threatening process as early as 1999.

The rescue program began in October 2024, when Aussie Ark collected adult snakes from the wild to create an “insurance population” in specialized enclosures. Eight juveniles were bred. Two were kept for their valuable genetics, and six were released beneath specially designed artificial rocks. These rocks, developed by researcher Benjamin Croak, copy the crevice size and heat-holding properties of natural stone, giving the young snakes a safe place to hide and warm themselves. Each snake has a unique head pattern, which allows researchers to identify individuals during regular surveys.

Supporters see the result as evidence that captive breeding can help species recover. Without intervention, they argue, a species with such slow reproduction might simply run out of time. The project also involves Indigenous rangers, who are being trained to monitor the snakes on their traditional lands, linking conservation with cultural knowledge. Professor Jonathan Webb, who has studied the species for 34 years, plans further releases at selected sites over the next few years.

However, reintroduction is far from a guaranteed solution. Released animals have no experience of the wild and can be eaten by native predators such as kookaburras and brown snakes, or by introduced cats and foxes. Four survivors after a few months is encouraging, but it says little about whether the snakes will live long enough to breed, which is the real measure of success. Captive breeding is also expensive, and a common criticism is that the money might be better spent protecting habitat, since releasing animals into an environment that is still being damaged may only delay their decline.

Webb himself identifies habitat loss as the greatest threat. He has called for a permit system that would require sellers of landscaping rock to prove their stone was not taken from the habitat of threatened species. Such a rule would place part of the responsibility on ordinary consumers, many of whom have no idea that a decorative boulder in their garden may once have been a snake’s home.

The story of the broad-headed snake illustrates a wider challenge in conservation. Saving a species is rarely a matter of one dramatic action; it usually requires science, money, cooperation and changes in everyday behavior. Snakes may not attract the same public sympathy as koalas or pandas, but the program raises an important question: should we judge a species’ value by how appealing it looks, or by the role it plays in the ecosystem it belongs to?

words.def: easily harmed or affected by something bad
words.ex: Young children are especially vulnerable to extreme heat.

words.def: action taken to improve a difficult situation or stop it getting worse
words.ex: Early intervention helped the student catch up with her reading.

words.def: to make sure that something will certainly happen
words.ex: Hard work cannot guarantee success, but it makes success much more likely.

words.def: to show that something is true or explain it by giving examples
words.ex: The teacher used a simple experiment to illustrate how magnets work.

words.def: attractive or interesting
words.ex: A shorter school day sounds appealing, but it might mean longer holidays disappear.

words.def: (of a plant or animal) at serious risk of disappearing completely
words.ex: The endangered turtles lay their eggs on only a few beaches.

words.def: a long, steep slope or cliff at the edge of a high area of land
words.ex: We climbed the escarpment to see the whole valley below.

words.def: a young animal that is not yet fully grown
words.ex: Each juvenile in the zoo’s breeding program is weighed every week.

words.def: the state of being kept in a zoo, enclosure or other place instead of living freely
words.ex: Some birds learn to talk in captivity but never do so in the wild.

words.def: the act of returning a species to an area where it used to live
words.ex: The reintroduction of wolves changed how deer moved through the park.

keySentences.text: The number is small, but the result is being described as a world first for the species.
keySentences.note: The “but” balances a weakness (small numbers) against the significance (a world first). The whole article weighs hope against limits.

keySentences.text: Its biology makes it especially vulnerable: snakes take around five years to reach adulthood, and females breed only every two or three years.
keySentences.note: The colon introduces the reasons for the species’ vulnerability. Factual questions often ask for the evidence after a colon.

keySentences.text: A more surprising threat is human demand for garden decoration.
keySentences.note: This sentence shifts from natural threats to a human one. Notice “more surprising,” which signals the writer’s emphasis.

keySentences.text: These rocks, developed by researcher Benjamin Croak, copy the crevice size and heat-holding properties of natural stone, giving the young snakes a safe place to hide and warm themselves.
keySentences.note: The “-ing” clause explains the purpose of the artificial rocks. Purpose and function details are common TOEFL targets.

keySentences.text: However, reintroduction is far from a guaranteed solution.
keySentences.note: “However” introduces the limits of the program. The counter-argument usually follows the supporters’ paragraph.

keySentences.text: Saving a species is rarely a matter of one dramatic action; it usually requires science, money, cooperation and changes in everyday behavior.
keySentences.note: “Rarely” and “usually” are hedging words, showing a careful general claim rather than an absolute one.

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, why can even small losses take decades for the species to recover from?
opts: The snakes mature slowly, and females do not breed every year.
The snakes live in only a few cities around Sydney.
Their venom makes it difficult for them to find mates.
The lizards they eat are disappearing faster than they are.
questions.evidence: snakes take around five years to reach adulthood, and females breed only every two or three years
questions.why: Slow growth (about five years to adulthood) and infrequent breeding mean that lost snakes are replaced very slowly.
optWhy: Correct. This paraphrases “five years to reach adulthood” and “breed only every two or three years.”
Detail swapped: the snakes live in rocky escarpments, not in cities.
Not mentioned: venom is mentioned, but not linked to finding mates.
Not mentioned: the paragraph does not say the lizards are disappearing.

questions.q: According to paragraph 3, all of the following have harmed the broad-headed snake EXCEPT
opts: a long period of drought
the removal of rocks for gardens
competition from introduced lizards
bushfires in 2020
questions.evidence: Several pressures have pushed the species toward the edge.
questions.why: Drought, bushfires and bush-rock removal are all listed. Introduced lizards are not mentioned; lizards are the snakes’ food.
optWhy: Mentioned: “The severe drought of 2017 to 2019.”
Mentioned: bush rock “collected from the wild for landscaping.”
Correct. Introduced lizards are never mentioned; lizards are prey, not competitors.
Mentioned: “the bushfires of 2020 hit populations hard.”

questions.q: Why does the author mention that each snake has a unique head pattern?
opts: To show that the snakes are easy for predators to see
To explain why two snakes were kept for their genetics
To suggest that captive-bred snakes look different from wild ones
To explain how researchers can recognize individual snakes
questions.evidence: which allows researchers to identify individuals during regular surveys
questions.why: The head pattern is mentioned because it lets researchers tell individual snakes apart when they check on them.
optWhy: Not mentioned: nothing links the pattern to predators.
Detail swapped: the genetics point is a separate idea in the same paragraph.
Not mentioned: no comparison with wild snakes is made.
Correct. The pattern “allows researchers to identify individuals.”

questions.q: The word “measure” in paragraph 6 is closest in meaning to
opts: a law passed by a government
a standard used to judge something
a unit for recording length
an action taken to solve a problem
questions.evidence: which is the real measure of success
questions.why: Breeding is the true way to judge whether the program has succeeded, so “measure” means a standard for judging.
optWhy: Another meaning of the word: a “measure” can be a law, but here it describes success.
Correct. Breeding is the standard used to judge success.
Another meaning of the word: units such as meters are measures, but that does not fit “success.”
Another meaning of the word: “measures” can be actions, but this sentence is about judging results.

questions.q: What can be inferred from paragraph 6 about the program’s success so far?
opts: It is too early to know whether the releases will lead to a lasting population.
Most of the released snakes have already been eaten by cats and foxes.
It has proven that captive breeding works better than protecting habitat.
The surviving snakes have already started breeding in the wild.
questions.evidence: it says little about whether the snakes will live long enough to breed
questions.why: Survival for a few months does not show whether the snakes will breed, so the long-term result is still unknown.
optWhy: Correct. The real test, breeding, has not yet happened.
Contradiction: at least four of six survived, so most have not been eaten.
Too extreme: the paragraph raises doubts about captive breeding rather than proving it is better.
Contradiction: the text says it is unclear whether they will live long enough to breed.

questions.q: Which of the following best expresses the essential information in the highlighted sentence in paragraph 7? Incorrect choices change the meaning in important ways or leave out essential information.
questions.highlight: Such a rule would place part of the responsibility on ordinary consumers, many of whom have no idea that a decorative boulder in their garden may once have been a snake’s home.
opts: Most consumers know their garden rocks come from snake habitat but buy them anyway.
Consumers would be fined if a snake were found living in their garden.
The rule would make buyers share responsibility, although many do not realize garden rocks may come from snake habitat.
Ordinary consumers should be responsible for building new homes for snakes.
questions.evidence: Such a rule would place part of the responsibility on ordinary consumers
questions.why: The sentence says the permit rule would make consumers partly responsible, and that many of them do not know where decorative rocks come from.
optWhy: Contradiction: the sentence says many consumers “have no idea.”
Adds information: fines are never mentioned.
Correct. It keeps both parts: shared responsibility and consumers’ lack of awareness.
Changes the meaning: the rule is about buying rock, not about building homes for snakes.

speak.p: Some people think governments should spend money mainly on saving popular animals, such as pandas and koalas, because they attract public support. Others believe less attractive animals, like snakes and insects, deserve equal attention. Which view do you agree with, and why?
speak.hint: Choose a side → reason 1 (public support or ecosystem role) + example → reason 2 + example → conclusion.

write.p: Professor: In Australia, scientists bred endangered snakes in captivity and released them into the wild. Most survived their first months. Some conservationists say captive breeding is essential for species that reproduce slowly. Others argue that limited money should go to protecting habitat instead, because animals cannot survive if their homes keep disappearing. Which approach should receive more funding? Explain why. (Grace says: If we wait for habitat protection, some species will disappear first. Captive breeding buys time and keeps their genes safe.) (Omar says: Releasing animals into a damaged environment is like filling a bucket with a hole in it. We have to stop the habitat loss first.)
steps: State which approach you would fund, or how you would balance them.
Give a reason and a concrete example (slow breeding, rock removal, predators, cost).
Respond to Grace or Omar, building on part of their idea.
